No cash prize, yet this could be worth more than a grant: a paid government pilot and a route to a state contract. Applications close in 9 days.

The Government of Telangana is running the Telangana Innovation Startup Challenge 2026, and it is built around seven real problems its departments want solved. They range from cheaper, theft-resistant solar irrigation kits for deep borewells to rapid food-adulteration testing in hostels, satellite monitoring of lake encroachment, automated pothole mapping, needle-free anaemia screening, AI-based Telugu reading assessment and app-based crop mapping.

Winning teams get to pilot their solution with state departments, and a successful pilot can lead to long-term procurement. Shortlisted teams will also be showcased at the Invest Telangana Global Summit in December.

Startups, innovators, researchers, technology firms and academic institutions from anywhere in India can apply, as long as the solution fits one of the seven problem statements.

The tip founders miss: judges score problem relevance first, so write your application around the department's pain point and measurable impact, not around your product's feature list.

Last date: 30 November 2026

A €200K investment is on the table for one deep-tech founder, and entry is free. Deadline: 30 November.

The Hello Tomorrow Global Challenge is one of the largest international competitions for deep-tech startups. It runs 12 tracks, names around 800 startups as Deep Tech Pioneers and invites about 90 finalists to pitch at its summit in Amsterdam in June 2027, where the top pitch carries a €200K investment from DeepBright Ventures.

Even if you do not win, Pioneer status brings Investor Day meetings with more than 300 VCs and corporate investors, and track winners get coaching plus introductions to partners and customers.

Teams of two or more building on new science or complex engineering can apply, from proof of concept up to Series B. You do not need to be incorporated to apply, but you cannot be a subsidiary or spin-off of an existing company.

The catch: prize money is paid only once you are incorporated, travel and stay in Amsterdam are on you, and summit tickets need a refundable €99 deposit. Budget for that before you apply.

Up to ₹20 lakh, equity-free, plus a real Indian city as your first government customer. MoHUA has reopened this challenge.

The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, with MyGov, has reopened the AMRUT 2.0 India Pitch-Pilot-Scale Startup Challenge. It funds startups to pilot their technology with an urban local body and then scale it across cities.

The problem areas are broad: fresh-water systems, non-revenue water, sewerage and used-water reuse, urban flooding, water governance, air quality, municipal energy efficiency, smart street lighting and urban heat resilience.

Selected startups receive a grant of up to ₹20 lakh, mentoring, a ministry citation and MoHUA support to scale through industry and city partnerships. You must be a DPIIT-recognised startup with a solution that fits one of the 12 themes and can show measurable results in a field pilot.

What founders often miss: the money is not upfront. It comes in three tranches of ₹5 lakh, ₹7 lakh and ₹8 lakh, each released only when pilot milestones are met. Plan your cash flow for that.
